To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

T1 is determined by the rate of intermolecular interactions between macromolecular and water protons, T2 is determined by the exchange rate of water protons between bound and free states, and both T1 and T 2 are independent of NMR field strength.

the dominant factors affecting 1H tissue relaxation times are the tissue type and the NMR frequency, with the dominant mechanisms being intermolecular interactions between macromolecular surfaces and a single bound layer of hydration water, and exchange diffusion of water in and out of the hydration layer.

the 1H NMR relaxation of tissue is determined by the dynamic state of hydrogen in the system, and the dynamic state of tissue hydrogen is determined by the intermolecular interactions between the hydrogen in the system and the macromolecules of the tissue.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new generation of NMR contrast agents for use in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of tumors and other disease states.
the development of NMR methods for the non-invasive measurement of the physiological and biochemical properties of tissues.
the application of NMR techniques to the study of the structure of biological systems, particularly the structure of water in biological tissue.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the relaxation times of normal tissues are not known with sufficient precision to be useful for clinical diagnosis, but that they are sufficiently well defined for the design of future experiments and for the interpretation of results.
the dominant factors affecting T1 and T1/T2 are the type of tissue and the NMR frequency.
the dominant relaxation mechanism is the same for both T1 and T1, and that it is a function of the macromolecular structure of each tissue.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

T1 of all tissues is dominated by the frequency dependence of water exchange rates between bound and free water, while T2 is determined by the rate of exchange diffusion between bound and free phases.

the relaxation times of most normal human and animal tissues can be predicted with a high degree of confidence from the simple equation T1 = AV1.8, where T1 is in seconds and V is the NMR frequency in megahertz, with a standard deviation of about 20%.
tissue T1 is a sensitive indicator of tissue type, but not a reliable index of pathology, and that T2 is an insensitive indicator of tissue type and pathology.
The main takeaway from our work is that
T1 is frequency dependent, and that T1 and T1/2 are not independent of each other.
T1 is the dominant tissue parameter for NMR imaging, and T2 is not as important as has been thought.
the FETS model is the best explanation to date for tissue NMR behavior and the T1 and T1/T2 ratio can be used as tissue-specific indicators of the dynamic state and hydration of tissue.
